name: Carrow & Sons Waxed Drover Coat
description:
A full-length waxed cotton drover coat in dark tobacco or midnight green, cut long enough to cover the knee and wide enough to layer over a sweater or light armor. The silhouette is unapologetically traditional — storm collar, deep side-entry pockets, a back vent for riding or climbing. The wax finish sheds rain without membrane technology, just good old-fashioned textile chemistry applied to a tight-woven cotton canvas. It smells faintly of beeswax and machine oil.

Carrow & Sons has been operating out of a warehouse-district workshop in the Tier 2 belt since 2161. The coat is heavy, stiff when new, and breaks in over years of wear. Dock workers, outer-district beat cops, and stubborn middle-class types who distrust smart-fabric all wear it. It gets better with age in a way synthetic jackets never do.
what_it_says: You value durability over novelty. You've probably owned this coat for a decade and plan to own it for two more.
story_hooks: A dockworker's coat has a bloodstain on the inner lining that its current owner didn't put there — and the previous owner has been missing for three months.
Carrow & Sons is being bought out by a Tier 4 corponation that wants to move manufacturing offsite; the founding family is quietly sabotaging the deal.
The coat's wax formula is apparently based on a proprietary compound that a street chemist claims is being used in a very different product.
